response: I'm so sorry to hear about the loss of your baby. Losing a child is one of the most painful experiences a person can go through, and it's essential to acknowledge that your feelings are valid and normal. Allow yourself to grieve and process your emotions, whether it's sadness, anger, guilt, or any other feeling that arises. Consider reaching out to a support group, either online or in-person, where you can connect with others who have experienced a similar loss. Talking to a therapist or counselor can also provide a safe and non-judgmental space to explore your emotions and work through your grief. Additionally, take care of your physical health by getting enough rest, eating nutritious food, and engaging in activities that bring you comfort and relaxation. Remember, grief is a unique and individual experience, and there's no set timeline for healing. Be patient and kind to yourself as you navigate this difficult time. If you need immediate support, you can call a crisis hotline or reach out to a trusted friend or family member. Some resources that may be helpful include the National Pregnancy Loss Foundation, the Miscarriage Association, or the March of Dimes. Remember, you are not alone, and your baby will always be remembered and loved.

I have attempted to talk with him in order to resolve our issues; however, he never wants to talk and often blames me for everything. I’m always there when he needs my help. He tells me although I help him doesn’t mean that I am a good person. He always discredits me as a woman and it’s hurtful. I spend most day crying and feeling lonely. I am unhappy and unsure of what I need to do.

sentence: I recommend that you contact a domestic violence shelter in your area.
response: That sounds like a very hurtful situation. Unfortunately, without a batterers intervention course or a desire to change, the abuse cycle is unlikely to stop. I do not recommend that you try to leave on your own due that being the most dangerous time when in an abusive relationship. As an abuser, his goal is to control you whether it's through mental or verbal means. I recommend that you contact a domestic violence shelter in your area. I have worked closely with Harbor House of Central Florida and know they provide housing, transportation, and any other needed resources to women leaving an abusive relationship. There is help out there and you are not alone. If you need any additional resources in your area, please don't hesitate to contact me.

I've worked with this guy for about three years now, and I knew the first time I saw him that I was attracted. Over time, he became a very dear friend, and we talked about our relationship problems, family, dreams, and so on. There was always flirtation with us, and one day pretty recently, it progressed to making out. We agreed to keep it quiet, and we did, but in the back of my mind, I hoped it would become something more. It didn't, and three months later, I'm still not over it.
I'm trying so hard to maintain the friendship because that's what he wants. We're no longer in the same office, which I thought would help me get over these feelings, but we still talk about work, and he's constantly touching me, so I'm still very drawn to him. He's a hugger and such a sweet guy, so I find myself fantasizing all the time about what could have been and what could still be, but he's clearly not interested. He's younger than me and prefers model types, but I see him checking me out a lot, which gives me hope. How do I get him out of my system and still maintain the friendship?

sentence: It may take time, but with patience, self-reflection, and a focus on your own growth, you can work through these feelings and develop a more casual, friendship-based relationship with your coworker, or move on to more fulfilling connections.
response:
It's completely normal to feel this way, especially given the strong emotional connection and flirtation you've shared with your coworker. To get him out of your system, I would recommend taking a step back and acknowledging that his behavior, although affectionate, is not a clear indication of romantic interest. It's possible that he values your friendship and enjoys your company, but doesn't see you in a romantic light. 

To move forward, consider setting boundaries for yourself, such as limiting physical touch or personal conversations that may be fueling your fantasies. It may also be helpful to focus on nurturing other relationships and hobbies outside of work to shift your attention away from him. 

Rather than trying to maintain the friendship as it is, consider taking a break from regular communication or establishing a more platonic dynamic. This might mean not initiating conversations or meetings, and instead, letting him take the lead. It's essential to prioritize your own emotional well-being and recognize that it's okay to grieve the loss of a potential romance.

Remember that you deserve to be with someone who is genuinely interested in you and values you for who you are. It may take time, but with patience, self-reflection, and a focus on your own growth, you can work through these feelings and develop a more casual, friendship-based relationship with your coworker, or move on to more fulfilling connections.
